source: USDA ARS Grapevine Genetics & Breeding Research / Foundation Plant Services (FPS) UC Davis Virus Certification Program
title: Grapevine Leafroll Disease Complex (GLRaV-1 through GLRaV-11, Ampeloviridae / Closteroviridae)
content: Grapevine leafroll disease (GLD) is the most economically important and widespread viral disease of grapevines (Vitis vinifera L. and interspecific Vitis hybrids) worldwide, occurring in all major wine and table grape producing regions of the world (approximately 98% of commercial vineyards in some regions test positive for at least one GLRaV species). The disease is caused by a complex of at least 11 taxonomically distinct phloem-limited positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA) viruses classified in the genera Ampelovirus (family Closteroviridae, order Martellivirales: GLRaV-1, GLRaV-3, GLRaV-4, GLRaV-5, GLRaV-6, GLRaV-8, GLRaV-9, GLRaV-10, GLRaV-11), Vitivirus (family Betaflexiviridae: GLRaV-2), and Velarivirus (family Closteroviridae: GLRaV-7). Grapevine leafroll-associated virus 3 (GLRaV-3, Ampelovirus) is the most globally distributed, most genetically diverse, and most economically severe GLRaV species, accounting for approximately 70% of all GLD diagnoses in vineyards worldwide; GLRaV-1 and GLRaV-2 are the next most prevalent. Yield losses of 15-40% and reductions of 2-6 Brix in fruit sugar content are consistently recorded in affected vineyards, resulting in downgrading of fruit quality grade, reduced wine price points, and significant economic losses; additional losses include reduced vine vigor, delayed fruit ripening and color development in red-skinned cultivars, poor cold acclimation of buds and canes, and reduced grafting success of propagation material. The most characteristic diagnostic symptom of GLD appears on mature leaves of red-fruited grapevine cultivars (V. vinifera 'Cabernet Sauvignon', 'Merlot', 'Pinot Noir', 'Zinfandel', etc.) beginning approximately 4-6 weeks after bloom: interveinal areas of the lower (basal) canopy leaves develop a bright reddish-purple discoloration, while the leaf veins themselves remain characteristically green (this 'green veins on red leaves' pattern is highly diagnostic). As the season progresses toward harvest, the reddish-purple discoloration spreads upward through the canopy; the leaf margins roll downward (revolute) and inward, giving the leaf a cupped, curled appearance that is the origin of the disease name 'leafroll'. In advanced stages, necrotic patches develop in the reddened interveinal areas, leaves become brittle, and premature defoliation occurs 2-4 weeks before normal harvest. In white-fruited grape cultivars ('Chardonnay', 'Riesling', 'Sauvignon blanc', 'Pinot Gris'), the reddish-purple discoloration does not occur due to the absence of anthocyanin pigments in the epidermis; instead, GLD-affected white cultivars develop a subtle chlorotic yellow-green mottling with downward rolling leaf margins, which is easily confused with nutritional (magnesium, potassium) deficiency symptoms or grapevine fanleaf virus (GFLV) infection. Symptom expression is highly dependent on the GLRaV species, the Vitis cultivar genotype, the vine's overall physiological stress, and environmental conditions: some V. vinifera cultivars (e.g., 'Riesling', 'Sangiovese') show symptoms very weakly or remain 'latent carriers' even when heavily infected; native American Vitis species (V. riparia, V. rupestris, V. labrusca) and many rootstock cultivars are often tolerant or symptomless carriers of GLRaV viruses even when infected, making them hidden reservoirs of inoculum in vineyards. GLD is a graft-transmissible disease and is spread by two principal mechanisms: (1) long-distance, international, and regional spread occurs exclusively through human movement of infected grapevine planting material (dormant scion budwood, rootstock cuttings, and grafted nursery grapevines); because GLRaVs are phloem-limited, they are not seed-transmitted, not transmitted by pollen, and not mechanically transmitted by pruning shears, farm equipment, or normal handling. (2) local within-vineyard and between-vineyard spread is mediated by several species of phloem-feeding insect vectors in the order Hemiptera, suborder Auchenorrhyncha (the old 'Homoptera' group): soft scale insects (Coccidae, most important vectors globally: Parthenolecanium corni - European fruit lecanium, Pulvinaria vitis - cottony grape scale, Neopulvinaria innumerabilis - cottony maple scale, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum - citricola scale, Saissetia oleae - black scale); mealybugs (Pseudococcidae: Pseudococcus maritimus - grape mealybug, Ps. viburni - obscure mealybug, Planococcus ficus - vine mealybug, Pl. citri - citrus mealybug); and certain species of aphids (Aphididae: Aphis illinoisensis - grapevine aphid) and whiteflies (Aleyrodidae: Bemisia tabaci - in some tropical/subtropical regions). Transmission by scale insects and mealybugs is semi-persistent (non-circulative, non-propagative): virions are acquired from an infected vine's phloem during feeding of all instar stages, retained in the foregut/precibarium for up to 24-72 hours, and inoculated into a healthy vine's phloem during subsequent feeding; no latent period is required, adults and first-instar 'crawlers' are the most efficient vector life stages, and transmission rates increase with increasing vector population density and number of GLRaV species present in mixed infections. Natural spread without insect vectors (wind, rain, contact) does not occur. Management: there are no chemical or biological treatments available to 'cure' or eliminate GLRaV viruses from an already-infected grapevine; the entire management strategy is based on prevention, exclusion, and early detection/eradication. (1) The single most important management practice for GLD is to plant only certified, virus-tested grapevine nursery stock produced under government-mandated or industry-approved vine certification programs (Foundation Plant Services FPS at UC Davis, USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository NCGR-Corvallis, Canadian Food Inspection Agency CFIA vine certification, EU Vine Certification Directive 2005/43/EC, Wine Australia Certified Vine Scheme). Certified vines are produced by meristem tip culture combined with thermotherapy and/or cryotherapy to eliminate GLRaV and other grapevine viruses, followed by extensive virus-indexed testing via RT-PCR, ELISA, and next-generation sequencing (NGS) high-throughput sequencing (HTS) before release. (2) annual or biennial vineyard monitoring and virus testing: scout visually for GLD symptoms on red-fruited cultivars from fruit set through harvest; collect leaf petiole samples from vines showing suspicious symptoms and test using commercial ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) serological kits for GLRaV-1, GLRaV-2, GLRaV-3, and RT-PCR/NGS for all GLRaV species; in high-value vineyards, systematic grid-based or whole-block testing of every vine using RT-PCR-based pooled sampling strategies allows detection of low-incidence infections (below 0.5% block infection rate) before visual symptoms appear. (3) rogue and destroy infected vines when the within-block GLD incidence is less than approximately 15-20%: immediately remove any confirmed GLD-positive vine (entire vine with root system, not just top-worked scion) from the vineyard and destroy it (chip, burn, or landfill; do not compost because viruliferous scale crawlers may still be present on bark); replace with certified virus-tested vines only after a 6-12 month fallow period to allow any remaining viruliferous vectors to die out or emigrate. (4) vector management where within-block spread rates are documented: monitor scale insect and mealybug populations using pheromone traps, visual inspection, and double-sided sticky tape crawler traps on vine trunks; apply insecticide treatments targeting the mobile first-instar 'crawler' life stage because settled adult scales and mealybugs under their protective waxy test coverings are not susceptible to most insecticides. Effective insecticide classes against scale crawlers in FPS/USDA trials: horticultural mineral oils (dormant-season and in-season 1-2% applications; the backbone of organic vector control), narrow-range petroleum oil, insecticidal soap, neonicotinoids (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, acetamiprid, clothianidin - post-bloom applications to minimize pollinator exposure), pyrethroids (bifenthrin, cypermethrin - good crawler contact activity but very disruptive to beneficial parasitoids and predators of scales), IGRs (insect growth regulators: pyriproxyfen, buprofezin - very effective against crawler stages, soft on beneficials), and spirotetramat / spirodiclofen (tetronic/tetramic acid derivatives, excellent systemic scale activity with high beneficial insect safety). Augmentative biological control using commercially reared parasitoid wasps (Metaphycus helvolus, M. luteolus, Microterys flavus, Anagyrus pseudococci, Leptomastix dactylopii) and predatory ladybeetles (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri - mealybug destroyer, Rhyzobius lophanthae) provides a sustainable, non-disruptive alternative to insecticide-based vector management in organic and IPM production systems. (5) tolerance-based management at high GLD incidence (above 25%): where block GLD infection rates exceed 25-30%, rogueing alone is no longer economically viable because the cost of vine removal/replacement exceeds the yield/quality penalty from GLD. In this situation, maintain optimal vine nutrition (adequate potassium, magnesium, zinc), avoid excessive crop load (cluster thin to moderate crop levels), manage irrigation to avoid drought stress, apply foliar magnesium + potassium supplements, and maintain vector suppression programs to slow further within-block spread, while planning for a gradual whole-block replant with certified virus-tested vines over a 3-5 year period.
